_readme: Curated metadata for the chezmoi tools inventory, rendered by ~/.local/bin/tools-inventory.
Everything here is prose a generator cannot derive: what a tool is for, why it exists, its
flags, and which platforms it actually works on. Everything the generator CAN derive is
deliberately absent — line counts, whether a tool is deployed on this host, and whether its
tests exist are all read from disk at render time, so they cannot go stale here.
Platform sets are curated rather than parsed out of .chezmoiignore on purpose: that file is a
chezmoi template with hostname lists and an includeTemplate call, and a second parser for it
would drift silently and produce a confidently wrong platform column. The per-host column is
not curated — it comes from `chezmoi ignored` plus a filesystem check.
A script in the source tree with no entry here is still rendered, from its own header comment,
and reported in a drift banner at the top of the page. Add it here to give it a real card.

page.title: Tools in chezmoi
page.lede: Every command the dotfiles repo installs — what it does, why it exists, how it is invoked, and which platforms it runs on. Descriptions paraphrase each script's own header comment.
page.scopeIn: things you type. The ~/.local/bin commands, the sandbox-side commands, the Windows-only host scripts, and the packages behind them.
page.scopeOut: the Claude Code hooks under ~/.claude/hooks and the sandbox hooks (audit.sh, gh-pr-guard.sh) — that is the config surface, and /config-map renders it.

groups.title: Query & digest
groups.note: Four tools that exist for the same structural reason: the useful operation was reachable only through something correctly ask-listed (python3 -c, curl, ssh, a raw test runner). Each narrows the capability far enough that a blanket allow rule becomes defensible.

groups.title: Scheduled housekeeping
groups.note: Each runs unattended on a systemd-user timer, which is why containment and failure reporting are written into the scripts rather than into how they are called.

groups.title: Platform shims
groups.note: Compat layers, not tools with a UI. Each shadows a real name earlier on PATH and forwards; they exist because a platform quirk broke something upstream.

groups.title: Windows host scripts
groups.note: Deployed only on Windows (bin/ and Scripts/ are ignored everywhere else). Each fixes a defect in something that is not going to fix itself.

groups.title: Sandbox-side helpers
groups.note: Invoked by claude-sandbox rather than typed, but they are programs with their own CLIs and their own tests. All live in ~/.claude/sandbox/, which chezmoi skips on Windows.

groups.title: Packages & libraries behind the commands
groups.note: Not commands themselves — listed so the inventory accounts for where the code actually lives.

excluded._why: Real scripts in the source tree that are deliberately not inventory entries. Listed so drift detection stays quiet about them instead of reporting them every run.
excluded.reason: Claude Code hooks and sourced libraries — the config surface, not commands. vault-search is listed here because it has its own curated entry keyed to the sandbox image rather than the host.

tools.name: ct
tools.desc: Launch Claude Code in its own named tmux session — one session per Claude — so the Agent View picker can attach to it from another machine with tmux attach -t <name>.
tools.why: The session name is the sanitized basename plus the last six digits of a cksum of the launch path, so same-basename repos stay distinct and re-running ct in a directory resumes rather than duplicates (new-session -A).
tools.pre: ct [dir] # dir defaults to $PWD CT_CLAUDE_BIN=… # override the resolved claude binary

tools.name: cts
tools.desc: Sibling to ct: runs claude-sandbox in its own named tmux session, so Agent View captures a real tmux: locator — which survives a pane id going stale, where a wezterm: one does not.
tools.why: Names are deterministic per repo (+branch), so re-running attaches instead of duplicating and each worktree stays independently jumpable. The _cts zsh completion calls ctw --list-* over ssh with fail-fast flags and caches results under $XDG_CACHE_HOME/cts, so an unreachable host fails fast instead of hanging the shell.
tools.pre: cts [dir] [claude-sandbox args…] # local cts --ssh[=HOST] [REPO] [-b BRANCH] # native claude on HOST over ssh # HOST defaults to daniel-server ($CTS_REMOTE_HOST); also -H/--host # CTS_CACHE_TTL=45 completion cache lifetime, seconds

tools.name: ctw
tools.desc: Remote companion to cts --ssh. Resolves a repo name under $CTS_REMOTE_ROOTS, optionally into a per-branch git worktree, then hands off to ct. It never touches tmux itself.
tools.why: Because ct names its session from a cksum of the launch dir, every per-branch worktree becomes a distinct auto-resuming session that registers in Agent View for free. ctw also answers the queries cts --complete-* sends, so completion and launch resolve through the exact same code and cannot disagree.

tools.name: claude-sandbox
tools.desc: Launch Claude Code in a Docker-based "Pattern C" sandbox: per-repo image, audited tool use, a socket-proxy'd Docker socket, an optional read-only vault subset, and sibling repos mounted as clean main snapshots by default.
tools.why: On PATH as a symlink to ~/.claude/sandbox/claude-sandbox. Sources sandbox-lib.sh and sandbox-worktree.sh; picks up machine-specific values (e.g. CLAUDE_VAULT_DIR) from an optional ~/.config/claude/local.env, and forwards the 1Password SSH-agent socket — whose path differs on macOS — so commits inside the container stay signed.
tools.pre: claude-sandbox [OPTIONS] <repo-path> isolation -w/--worktree [NAME] branch claude/<NAME>, random suffix if omitted -b/--branch BRANCH keep the branch's own name (cannot combine with -w) --fresh/--new new conversation instead of auto --continue sessions --list --rename OLD NEW --prune (fzf) --gc (remote branch deleted) images --rebuild --rebuild-base --generate mounts --no-vault --no-chezmoi --no-work-config --no-repos --repos-live modes --shell interactive bash (execs into a live container if one is running); unaudited -x/--exec PROMPT headless implementer: progress → stderr, result → stdout between <<<EXEC_RESULT>>> markers

tools.name: spares
tools.desc: Tell claimed Claude sessions apart from idle pre-warmed spares.
tools.why: ps cannot do this: a session dispatched onto a spare keeps its --bg-spare argv, so every argv scan reports live working sessions as idle. The daemon roster is the only oracle, and its pid is the bg-pty-host rather than the worker underneath — so the join runs through the spare id shared by <id>.pty.sock and <id>.claim.sock. An unreadable roster exits 2 rather than defaulting to "spare", which is exactly the wrong answer this tool exists to prevent.
tools.pre: spares [--json] # test seams: SPARES_PROC_DIR SPARES_ROSTER SPARES_SESSIONS_DIR

tools.name: vault-search

badges.text: inside the sandbox only — not a host command

tools.desc: Query the curated, read-only vault index mounted into a sandbox. The launcher builds a DuckDB index over only the allowlisted vault pages and mounts it at $SANDBOX_VAULT_DB; the embedding model and the FTS extension are baked into the image, so this runs fully offline.

tools.name: claude-rc-resume
tools.desc: Resume a Remote Control session from the terminal by its name.
tools.why: A session the claude rc host spawns from the phone lives in its own git worktree, and Claude Code keys the transcript by that directory, so it appears in claude --resume only from inside .claude/worktrees/<name>/. When the phone drops, getting the session back meant finding that directory by hand; this does the finding.

tools.name: effort
tools.desc: Get or set Claude Code's effortLevel in ~/.claude/settings.json without opening a session.
tools.why: effortLevel is a runtime-owned key that /effort writes live and claude-settings-merge carries across chezmoi apply, so editing it here is equivalent — and a fresh claude-sandbox launch picks it up.

tools.name: stash-mine
tools.desc: Touch only the git stash entries this worktree created.
tools.why: The stash stack is shared across every worktree of a repo, and a bare git stash pop once applied another session's 25-file WIP. The safe protocol — push with a unique tag, apply and drop by SHA, never pop — is correct but easy to get wrong by hand; this carries it out.

tools.name: planka

badges.text: chezmoi deploys it everywhere; soft-fails without the macOS keychain

tools.desc: Record Claude Code session work on the local Planka board.
tools.why: It sits on the PostToolUse and Stop paths, so every expected failure exits 0 with a line in the log: it must never fail an edit or block a stop. The Planka password lives in the macOS login keychain, the same pattern the work overlay uses for its other keys.

tools.name: pr-dash

badges.text: elsewhere it prints the URL instead of opening it

tools.desc: Launch the PR dashboard in ~/.local/share/pr-dash on a loopback port and open it in the browser. If the launchd agent or another run is already serving, it only opens the page.

tools.name: jsonq
tools.desc: Query JSON with a closed subset of Python syntax — Python syntax over already-parsed JSON, sitting between jq (which runs out of road quickly) and arbitrary code execution.
tools.why: What makes Bash(jsonq:*) defensible is not a check, it is an absence: the file contains no eval, no exec, no compile. ast.parse builds a tree that executes nothing; the dispatch tables are the grammar, so a node type with no entry cannot run. There is no ast.Attribute handler at all, so x.y is refused in every position — no method calls, no module namespaces, no __class__. The reachable object graph is exactly JSON values, the fixed function table, and lambdas defined by the query. This deliberately reverses an earlier design that enumerated forbidden nodes and then handed the source to eval; every escape lived in the gap between the checker and the more permissive second evaluator.
tools.pre:
jsonq 'sorted(d["permissions"])' settings.json
jsonq '[r for r in d["rules"] if r["on"]]' a.json
jsonq 'set(d1) - set(d2)' a.json b.json
jsonq --script 'out = [x["id"] for x in d if x["ok"]]' a.json
jsonq --jsonl 'len([x for x in d if x["type"] == "user"])' session.jsonl

flags.label: Function table:
flags.html: builtins (len sorted sum min max zip enumerate map filter) · dict/list helpers (keys values items get merge unique flatten counter groupby) · strings (lower upper strip split join replace startswith) · regex (re_test re_search re_groups re_findall re_sub re_split) · math & stats (floor ceil sqrt log mean median) · dumps / loads

flags.label: Gotcha:
flags.html: invoke by name, never as python3 jsonq — claude-guard's deny rules (deny.py) read an interpreter keyword next to a .key/.env/.pem substring as a secrets read, and JSON field names trip it.

tools.name: otelq
tools.desc: Query the local Loki / Prometheus telemetry stack without a permission prompt. Output is JSON on stdout so it composes with jsonq; --rows renders the common "value ⇥ labels" shape instead.
tools.why: curl:* prompts because curl takes an arbitrary URL and can write the response to disk — an exfiltration and a download primitive in one. Neither is available here: the host is not an argument, every request is a GET to 127.0.0.1 on two fixed ports, and the response only ever reaches stdout. The caller controls a LogQL/PromQL string, and neither language can execute a process, read a file, or reach the network.
tools.pre:
otelq logs 'sum by (event_name) (count_over_time({service_name="claude-code"}[19h]))'
otelq logs '{service_name="claude-code"} | event_name=`api_error`' --stream --limit 5
otelq metric 'sum by (model) (increase(claude_code_cost_usage_USD_total[19h]))'
otelq labels --name service_name
otelq ready

flags.label: Backends:
flags.html: the claude-otel docker-compose stack in the same repo — OTel collector, Loki, Prometheus, Tempo, Grafana.

tools.name: tq
tools.desc: Run a command, print a compact digest, keep the full result as JSON. The runner's exit code is always preserved and its argv is passed through untouched.
tools.why: Linters are digested as findings rather than a pass rate — silence about a line is not an assertion that the line is good, so there is no denominator to report. Sweeps get a count, a histogram and an evenly spaced sample, plus the two ways a count misleads stated in the headline: it is a floor when the command capped itself (git log -n 50 returning 50), and it is not a count of anything when the command failed part-way. A sweep small enough to print is printed whole. A command that does something — find -delete, git commit — is never claimed.
tools.pre: tests node --test · pytest (uv run / python -m) · go test · cargo test gradle test · mvn test · prek run --all-files linters ruff check · mypy · eslint · tsc --noEmit · shellcheck · go vet · cargo clippy sweeps find · fd · ls -R · rg --files · git ls-files · rg/grep · git diff · git log

flags.label: Flags
flags.html: (before the command): --scope=all|file|added — which findings reach the digest · --diff-base=<ref> (default HEAD) · --retry — one more go, survivors marked FLAKY (node/pytest only, skipped above 10 failures) · --flaky-result=pass · --ingest=rdjson|sarif|ruff-json|shellcheck-json1

flags.label: Env:
flags.html: TQ_JSON (where the structured result lands) · TQ_TIMEOUT (0 = unbounded; a run past it is killed and reported TIMED OUT) · TQ_SCOPE · TQ_DIFF_BASE · TQ_RETRY · TQ_RETRY_MAX_FAILURES. A failed run also leaves the runner's unparsed output at <json>.raw.

flags.label: The hook's reason:
flags.html: a node --test run prints ~65 KB nobody reads when nothing is wrong. In a git hook that is noise; in an agent's Bash call it is context, spent at the same rate whether or not anything failed, and spent again by every parallel agent running the same suite.

tools.name: otel-sweep
tools.desc: Read the Claude Code telemetry stack on every machine, unprompted.
tools.why: The same reason as otelq, one layer out. Once the question became "and what about daniel-box and daniel-server?", the only tools that could answer were ssh and curl, both ask-listed for good reason. This answers it without widening either.

tools.name: dotsync
tools.desc: Manifest-driven dotfiles preservation subsystem. Zero dependencies — node builtins only — with the pure core separated from IO behind an injectable runner, so it is unit-testable against fixtures.

tools.name: claude-settings-merge
tools.desc: Deep-merge JSON fragments left→right: objects merge by key, arrays concat and de-dupe by JSON value, a later scalar wins, a missing file is treated as {}.
tools.why: Two refusals are load-bearing. A shape conflict is refused rather than resolved by guesswork — taking the overlay is how {"permissions": null} silently produced a settings file with no permission model at all, at exit 0. And __proto__ is handled explicitly: JSON.parse makes it an own property, but out[k] = … hits Object.prototype's setter, so a fragment carrying __proto__ once set the accumulator's prototype and produced permission rules present in no visible key of any input.

tools.name: terminal-cheatsheet

badges.text: run by hand — nothing runs it on apply

tools.desc: Regenerate a single-page HTML cheatsheet of this machine's terminal, Neovim, Yazi and Claude Code keybinds — parsed from the deployed config files, so it reflects what is actually running after template rendering.
tools.why: Cross-platform by parsing whatever is present: WezTerm on Windows, Ghostty on macOS/Linux, Neovim and Yazi everywhere, Claude keybinds wherever ~/.claude/keybindings.json exists. Under WSL it also probes /mnt/c/Users/*/.config/wezterm/wezterm.lua, so the Linux sheet still shows the binds you type in the host terminal. Dependency-free; the parsers are format-driven rather than entry-driven, so new keybinds flow through automatically.
tools.pre: terminal-cheatsheet [output.html] # or TERMINAL_CHEATSHEET_OUT=… # honors $XDG_CONFIG_HOME and $YAZI_CONFIG_HOME

tools.name: tools-inventory

badges.text: run by hand — nothing runs it on apply

tools.desc: Generates this page. Discovers the tool roster from the chezmoi source tree, merges it with the curated prose in tools.json, and derives every volatile fact — line counts, which platform column applies, whether each tool is deployed on this host — at render time.
tools.why: It reads the source rather than the deployed tree because the roster has to include tools this machine does not get: a Fedora box would otherwise render an inventory with the Windows scripts silently missing. The per-host column comes from chezmoi ignored, which is chezmoi evaluating its own templates, plus a filesystem check — never from a second parser for .chezmoiignore. A script in the source tree with no tools.json entry is still rendered from its own header comment and reported in a drift banner, so adding a tool cannot silently leave the page incomplete.
tools.pre: tools-inventory [output.html] # or TOOLS_INVENTORY_OUT=… tools-inventory --check # report drift, write nothing; exit 1 if any # TOOLS_INVENTORY_SOURCE=… chezmoi source dir (default: `chezmoi source-path`)

flags.label: Idempotent:
flags.html: the rendered page carries no timestamp, so an unchanged inventory produces a byte-identical file and the generator skips the write. Re-running it costs nothing when nothing has changed.

tools.name: claude-guard
tools.desc: CLI entry for the claude_guard package: explain, replay, segment. Not a hook — the hook shims in ~/.claude/hooks carry the per-event failure contracts; this one is for a human or a test, so a missing interpreter is an error rather than a silent no-decision.

tools.name: prompt-friction
tools.desc: Measure how many Bash calls that interrupted you would now answer themselves.
tools.why: Claude Code's OTEL stream records who decided each tool call: a config rule, a hook, or user — a prompt someone had to answer. This reads the user ones out of Loki and replays each through today's PermissionRequest hook chain, so "did that auto-approver change help?" is a command rather than an afternoon.

tools.name: grafana-mcp

badges.text: spawned by the Claude desktop app as an MCP server

tools.desc: Launch mcp-grafana with the Grafana service-account token attached, read from the login keychain.
tools.why: The desktop app spawns stdio MCP servers directly, not through an interactive shell, so the precmd hook that normally exports the token never fires. mcp-grafana then reported itself connected and returned HTTP 401 on every call.

tools.name: stdio-blocking

badges.text: prefixed by the homelab repo's uv-python.sh hook

tools.desc: Clear O_NONBLOCK on fds 0, 1 and 3, called as a bare prefix (stdio-blocking; <cmd>).
tools.why: Every ansible CLI refuses to start on non-blocking stdio, and the Claude Code Bash tool hands its child a file with O_NONBLOCK set. The homelab server repo prepends this to every command that runs ansible or the system python.

tools.name: retention-sweep
tools.desc: Sweeper over retention-manifest.json: for every row, report how many entries currently match its glob and their combined size. With --apply it also acts.
tools.why: Five containment rules, plus a floor. Acting requires --apply; a row acts only if it is in the source-literal APPLY_ROWS, never derived from the manifest, so adding a manifest row cannot grant itself a delete path; every removal must resolve underneath its own glob's literal prefix, and symlinks are refused outright; an unparseable cap is a refusal, not a default; and flock means a hook-fired run colliding with the timer exits quietly. Under all of it, nothing younger than its row's grace is ever eligible. Rotation is separate on purpose — rewriting a file a live process holds open is a different failure mode, so rotate-size and truncate-lines rows need --apply and --rotate together, and the hourly timer passes only --apply.
tools.pre: retention-sweep # pure report (default) retention-sweep --apply # removal rows in APPLY_ROWS retention-sweep --apply --rotate # plus ROTATE_ROWS; manual only

flags.label: Portability:
flags.html: the script itself is portable; only its scheduling is systemd-specific — it runs by hand anywhere.

tools.name: reap-backgrounded-origins-sweep
tools.desc: Reap the redundant interactive origin left running behind every backgrounded Claude session. For each live session it reads the worker cmdline by pid and, only on the exact backgrounding signature, SIGTERMs the origin.
tools.why: Deliberately independent of the Claude daemon's hook config, which goes stale until the daemon restarts — this is the daemon-independent supplement to the reap-backgrounded-origin.sh hook, sharing reap-origin-lib.sh so detection and guards are identical. Since Claude Code 2.1 a backgrounded session is dispatched onto a pre-warmed spare whose argv keeps no --resume link, so the cmdline scan alone silently stopped reaping; a roster pass covers that dispatch.

tools.name: claude-changelog-watch
tools.desc: Unattended daily /changelog-watch run, Linux side. The macOS half is a launchd plist driving work-laptop-config's run-skill.sh; neither travels here, so this is a purpose-built runner for the one command.

tools.name: claude-transcript-scan
tools.desc: Find credentials that have already landed in a session transcript.
tools.why: The preventive half is block-dangerous-bash.sh, which denies a command before it runs. It cannot close the whole gap, because no hook can rewrite a tool result — so a secret a command printed stays in the transcript, and this is the sweep that finds it.

tools.name: flatpak-update
tools.desc: Update user-scope flatpaks, then remove the runtimes nothing references any more.
tools.why: Flathub is served badly over the Mullvad tunnel, so the fetch runs through mullvad-exclude when that works. That detour is why this is a script rather than two ExecStart lines, and a script means "update my flatpaks now" is the same command the timer runs.

tools.name: mullvad-settings-watch
tools.desc: Daily check that the Mullvad tunnel settings which cost throughput (DAITA, entry relay) have not drifted back. Findings raise a desktop notification and fail the unit.

tools.name: otel-savings-rollup
tools.desc: Append one day of tooling-cost figures (otelq savings all) to a durable file.
tools.why: Loki keeps 31 days, and a stack rebuild has already lost every day older than a week once. Anything that compares a number against the same number a quarter ago has to keep its own copy.

tools.name: otel-sweep-watch
tools.desc: Daily check that every machine is actually exporting telemetry, built on otel-sweep.
tools.why: The failure is silent by construction: a session started before its collector was up exports nothing for its whole life while pods stay green. Two went unnoticed for three days each, so findings raise a desktop notification.

tools.name: audio-sink-toggle

badges.text: chezmoi deploys it everywhere; inert without pactl

tools.desc: Cycle the default PipeWire sink and drag every playing stream along with it.
tools.why: Setting the default sink only affects new streams — anything already playing stays on the old device, which is what makes a naive set-default-sink feel broken. Moving the existing sink-inputs is what makes the switch immediate. Sinks are matched by name rather than numeric id, because ids are reassigned whenever a device suspends or reconnects; an unknown current sink (headset powered off) falls through to the first entry rather than failing. Replaces the Ctrl+F11 AutoHotkey binding the Stream Deck "Audio" key used on Windows.

tools.name: streamcontroller-health
tools.desc: Restart StreamController when it is alive but has lost the deck.
tools.why: It fails in two shapes and systemd only sees one. If it aborts outright (the libdbus dbus_watch_handle() assertion, SIGABRT) the process exits and Restart=on-failure handles it. The other shape is the problem: it fails to grab the deck with a TransportError and then keeps running with no page loaded — a perfectly healthy service to systemd, a dark Stream Deck to you. So the health signal is deliberately not "is the process alive", which is exactly the state being detected; it is "does StreamController hold the deck's USB node". That emphasis was found the hard way: fuser reports the node busy whenever a Wine prefix is running, because winedevice.exe opens every USB device it can see — so asking "is anything holding it" reported a healthy deck for as long as a game was open.

tools.name: streamdeck-usb-reset
tools.desc: Issue a USBDEVFS_RESET to the Elgato Stream Deck.
tools.why: When StreamController dies from the libdbus assertion it aborts inside libusb's transaction, leaving the device mid-transfer while still enumerated. That combination is the trap: the deck still shows up in lsusb, so a plain relaunch looks like it should work and instead fails with Failed to write feature report (-1), which upstream does not treat as fatal. The process keeps running with no page loaded, squatting the USB handle, and every further relaunch stacks another deckless instance behind it. Resetting the device between the crash and the relaunch turns "relaunch and hope" into deterministic recovery. Exits 0 whenever there is nothing to do, so it is safe as an unconditional ExecStartPre= — most starts are ordinary logins, not recoveries.

tools.name: wezterm-pane-ssh
tools.desc: Print the argv of the ssh client backing a WezTerm pane, one argument per line, or nothing when the pane is not ssh'd anywhere.
tools.why: WezTerm cannot answer this for a WSL pane — it only ever sees wslhost.exe, and OSC 7 is swallowed by tmux, so an Agent View homelab jump is invisible from the Windows side. $WEZTERM_PANE is the one handle that crosses, and it is readable from /proc. Two layouts are resolved: direct (ssh is a descendant of the pane shell) and tmux (ssh is a child of the tmux server, with a stale inherited $WEZTERM_PANE, so the pane's tmux client is mapped to its session instead).
tools.pre: wezterm-pane-ssh <wezterm-pane-id> # exit status advisory; no output = not remote

tools.name: tmux-askpass
tools.desc: SUDO_ASKPASS helper for hosts with no graphical session — the headless counterpart to the ksshaskpass branch in ~/.zshenv.
tools.why: A shell with no controlling terminal (Claude Code's ! commands, ssh host cmd) has nowhere to prompt, so sudo refuses rather than asking. There is no desktop to draw a dialog on, but the tmux session the work already happens in can: display-popup reads the password with echo off and hands it back over a FIFO. Nothing is weakened — the password is still required and /etc/sudoers is untouched. The password never touches disk: the FIFO lives under $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (tmpfs, 0700) and is passed by pipe rather than argv or environment, so no other process can read it out of ps.

tools.name: bt-hid-kick
tools.desc: Recover a wedged Bluetooth mouse right now, from a hardware key. A wedged HID-over-GATT device reads Connected with a live battery but has no input node, so there is no pointer; the bt-hid-health timer recovers it too, but on a 2-minute cycle.

tools.name: desk-away
tools.desc: Lock the session and blank every display — the "leaving the desk" key — and wake them on a second press.
tools.why: Blanking rather than disabling outputs: measured on the 3080 Ti, DPMS-off drops the GPU from P0 / 92 W to P8 / 12.6 W, and disabling outputs saves no more than that while costing a window reshuffle.

tools.name: mic-mute-toggle
tools.desc: Toggle mute on the default PipeWire source. Unlike the Discord plugin's mute key, this mutes the capture device itself, so it covers Meet, Zoom, OBS and anything else holding the mic.

tools.name: clip-bridge
tools.desc: Serve this desktop's clipboard images to an SSH session on another host, so Claude Code running there can answer Ctrl+V. The remote half is the xclip shim, which proxies Claude's two clipboard reads back here over an ssh RemoteForward.

tools.name: clip2server
tools.desc: Put the Wayland clipboard's image onto daniel-box and hand its remote path to the Claude session running there. Claude Code resolves a typed image path into a real attachment, which a terminal paste of image bytes cannot do.

tools.name: login-window-layout
tools.desc: Open the everyday app set at login, one per monitor. Placement comes from the "login placement" rules in kwinrulesrc, except for Firefox, which this script places itself because every Firefox window shares one wmclass.

tools.name: mx-ergo-pointer
tools.desc: Apply pointer acceleration to the Logitech MX Ergo S and nothing else, matching the device by vendor and product id. KWin persists the setting into kcminputrc, so it survives reboots.

tools.name: mx-ergo-solaar
tools.desc: Assert the MX Ergo S button and wheel state that hold-to-precision needs. None of it can live on the device, which has no onboard profiles, so every setting is re-applied by software on each connect.

tools.name: mx-ergo-watch
tools.desc: Re-run mx-ergo-pointer and mx-ergo-solaar whenever KWin reports the trackball (re)appearing. It is Bluetooth, so it can show up long after login.

tools.name: mx-ergo-resync
tools.desc: Re-assert the MX Ergo S's full intended state after something else changed it.
tools.why: Logi Options+ on another machine diverts the controls it manages, the scroll wheel included, and diversion is device state rather than host state. Back on this machine the wheel stays diverted and scrolling is dead until something re-asserts it.

tools.name: wpe
tools.desc: Control linux-wallpaperengine: pick a wallpaper, pick a screen, start and stop the background service.
tools.why: Wallpaper Engine itself is Windows-only and does not work under Proton. This drives Almamu/linux-wallpaperengine, a native reimplementation that reads the Steam-installed content directly.
tools.pre:
wpe pick | list | outputs | set | screen | fps | layer | scaling
wpe watch start|stop|enable|disable|once|log|status

tools.name: wpe-pick

badges.text: launched by wpe pick · desktop entry

tools.desc: Thumbnail picker for linux-wallpaperengine. Every change goes back through wpe, so the picker is a view over it rather than a second owner of the same state.

tools.name: wpe-watch
tools.desc: Restart the wallpaper renderer when the set of connected displays changes. linux-wallpaperengine resolves its screens once at start, so after a KVM switch the wallpaper is missing on every display that was absent then.

tools.name: fix-games-mount
tools.desc: Repair the NTFS Steam volume at /mnt/games after a hard reset leaves it dirty, then bring its systemd mount and any dependent bind mount back up. With no flag it checks only and writes nothing.

tools.name: logi-dev-mgr-kick

badges.text: chezmoi deploys it everywhere; exits 0 without the launchd agent

tools.desc: Restart Logi Options+'s device manager so it re-finds the trackball.
tools.why: The MX Ergo keeps working while it disappears from the Options+ device list, because macOS drives the pointer from the receiver's boot-protocol interface. The mouse still moving reads as proof the stack is healthy, which sends the hunt to permissions or a reinstall instead of the one process that lost it.

tools.name: mac-askpass
tools.desc: The macOS SUDO_ASKPASS helper: a shell with no controlling terminal (Claude Code's ! commands, ssh host cmd, launchd agents) gets osascript's secure password dialog instead of a sudo refusal. The Aqua counterpart of tmux-askpass.

tools.name: jq
tools.desc: LF shim for the winget/official Windows jq, which opens stdout in text mode so every \n becomes \r\n. The trailing CR corrupts values in bash pipelines — agentview's @tsv rows split wrong, hook captures keep a stray CR. -b opens jq's streams in binary mode. Named jq (no extension) so it shadows jq.exe without recursing; exec means no extra fork and exit codes, streaming and binary output are preserved.

flags.label: Gating:
flags.html: native jq on macOS and Linux already emits LF, so the shim would be pure overhead there — it is gated off in .chezmoiignore.

tools.name: sudo
tools.desc: Supplies -A when there is no terminal to prompt on.
tools.why: sudo(8)'s ENVIRONMENT section says SUDO_ASKPASS names the helper used "if no terminal is available or if -A is specified" — on Ubuntu 24.04 (sudo 1.9.15p5) only the second half holds. Measured on daniel-box 2026-08-01: with SUDO_ASKPASS exported and verified present, plain sudo ls still refused with "a terminal is required to read the password", while -A drew the tmux popup and succeeded. Everything else passes through untouched, and an invocation that already chose its own input method (-A, -S, -n) is left alone.

flags.label: Gating:
flags.html: deliberate — shadowing sudo in PATH is not something to deploy onto a workstation that never asked for it, least of all a work machine.

tools.name: xclip

badges.text: no ignore rule, so it lands everywhere; needs wl-copy to do anything

tools.desc: Forward X11 clipboard calls to WSLg's wl-copy/wl-paste, which bridge to the Windows clipboard. Needed because /etc/wsl.conf sets appendWindowsPath=false (so clip.exe is off PATH) and the real xclip/xsel are not installed.
tools.why: Two extras beyond a plain forward, both for Claude Code's image paste: the TARGETS probe is answered with wl-paste -l (the old shim ignored -t and dumped raw bytes, so Claude's grep image/* matched nothing), and a request for image/png with only a bmp present is converted on the fly.

tools.name: wl-bmp2png

badges.text: deployed everywhere; only WSLg produces the bmp it converts

tools.desc: Convert a BMP on stdin to a PNG on stdout, stdlib only, no Pillow. WSLg mirrors the Windows clipboard image only as image/bmp, but Claude Code and the API accept png/jpeg/gif/webp. Handles the 24- and 32-bit BITMAPINFOHEADER bitmaps WSLg emits and exits non-zero on anything else, so the xclip shim falls back cleanly.

tools.name: tasklist.exe

badges.text: no caller since agentview was removed

tools.desc: Symlinks into /mnt/c/Windows/System32 — taskkill was how agentview ended a Windows pane. Deployed only on WSL (a Linux kernel reporting "microsoft"); anywhere else they would be dangling.

tools.name: discord

badges.text: falls through to the real binary without a working mullvad-exclude

tools.desc: Launch Discord outside the Mullvad tunnel.
tools.why: Cloudflare intermittently serves Discord's "Temporary Network Error" page to shared Mullvad exit addresses whose reputation has drifted — a flat 403 with nothing solvable client side. The only local lever is which address the request leaves from.

tools.name: steam

badges.text: falls through to the real binary without a working mullvad-exclude

tools.desc: Launch Steam outside the Mullvad tunnel.
tools.why: Games built on ISteamNetworkingSockets need NAT hole-punch probes to reach the client, and Mullvad's exit drops them upstream of this machine, so no local firewall rule can undo it.

tools.name: TaskbarAutoHideFix
tools.desc: Fixes the Windows 11 taskbar auto-hide breakage after resume/unlock that ExplorerPatcher's per-monitor taskbars amplify. On wake, Windows recreates the taskbar and its auto-hide app-bar registration collides with a stale one, which both pops a "you can have only one auto-hide toolbar per side" dialog and flips auto-hide back off.
tools.why: The collision can land a second or two after the trigger fires, so a single re-assert gets clobbered — hence a short retry window. Each pass closes any #32770 dialog that is the auto-hide popup and, if auto-hide is off (or a popup was present), re-asserts it off→on to force a clean app-bar re-registration.

tools.name: wsl-shutdown.cmd
tools.desc: Instantly stop the WSL2 VM to free all its RAM and CPU — e.g. before launching a game. WSL relaunches on next use; everyday cache give-back is already automatic via autoMemoryReclaim in .wslconfig.

tools.name: streamdeck-watcher
tools.desc: Restarts the Elgato Stream Deck app whenever the device (re)appears on USB. Elgato's software will not reconnect on its own after the device drops and comes back, which leaves it stuck on the Elgato logo with no buttons after boot, resume from hibernate, a KVM switch back, or a monitor USB hub dropping power when the panel sleeps.

tools.name: wslhost-interop-reaper
tools.desc: Kills wslhost.exe processes that have leaked spinning interop threads.
tools.why: microsoft/WSL#41173 — open, and present in every release through 2.9.4. ProcessInteropMessages re-issues its ReadFile forever when the read completes synchronously with zero bytes; all three loop exits sit inside if (!Success), and a gracefully-closed hvsocket returns success with BytesRead == 0, so the thread spins at a full core inside NtReadFile.

tools.name: sonar-routing-watcher
tools.desc: Keeps SteelSeries Sonar's playback channels pointed at the Arctis stereo Game endpoint. Sonar silently reassigns them to the mono Chat endpoint whenever a KVM switch re-enumerates the headset's USB base station in the wrong order.

tools.name: compact-session.py
tools.desc: Compact a Claude Code sandbox session into structured data. extract parses the session JSONL to JSON; summarize calls the Claude API for a summary; render writes the vault note and prints its index one-liner.

tools.name: exec-stream.py
tools.desc: Filter for claude-sandbox --exec: reads --output-format stream-json events, emits human-readable progress to stderr as it goes, and writes the final result to stdout between <<<EXEC_RESULT>>> markers so an orchestrator can extract it without scraping the stream. Exit code reflects the implementer's success.

tools.name: gen-vault-index.py
tools.desc: Build the DuckDB index over the allowlisted vault subset that vault-search queries; and the socket-proxy filter that decides which container-create requests the sandbox's Docker socket will pass.

tools.name: vault-index
tools.desc: local hybrid-search index over the Markdown vault, retrieving by meaning + keyword instead of routing through index.md summaries. Vault-agnostic; build/query find nothing rather than erroring when no vault is configured. Backs vault-search.

tools.name: config-map
tools.desc: deterministic generator for the Claude Setup Map, one self-contained collapsible HTML page at $CLAUDE_VAULT_DIR/Meta/Claude_Setup_Map.html. Vault-optional. Driven by the /config-map skill.

tools.name: githooks
tools.desc: pre-commit, pre-push, and secrets-check.js.

tools.name: claude-audit-portable
tools.desc: gen-install.js + install.sh + package, for carrying the audit tooling to another machine.

tools.name: tq libs
tools.desc: ~/.local/share/tq/ — detect.py, digest.py, result.py, scope.py, node-reporter.mjs, plus the adapters/ and runners/ packages.

tools.name: canon.py
tools.desc: canonicalize an input before deciding on it. "A guard that inspects one form of an input while its consumer acts on another is not a guard." Two families: keys (Go's encoding/json matches struct fields case-insensitively, so a filter reading Python dict keys exactly is vacuous against {"hostconfig": …}) and target (an HTTP router decodes percent-escapes before routing, so a filter matching the raw request-target never sees /containers/%63reate).

tools.name: sandbox libs
tools.desc: sandbox-lib.sh, sandbox-worktree.sh, sandbox-worktree-ops.sh, sandbox-worktree-gc.sh, sandbox-mounts.sh, sandbox-image.sh, sandbox-proxy.sh, sandbox-auth.sh, sandbox-session.sh, sandbox-compact.sh, resolve-sandbox-settings.sh — all sourced by claude-sandbox, none executed. The worktree helpers are pure functions of their arguments with no exit calls, which is what lets the launcher and the tests both source the file. sandbox-mounts.sh deliberately is not pure — its functions append to the launcher's DOCKER_ARGS and read its globals, so sourcing it requires the launcher's variable context.

tools.name: claude-otel
tools.desc: the docker-compose stack otelq queries: OTel collector, Loki, Prometheus, Tempo, Grafana.
